note: Adjudicated variants: 9 accidental (punctuation, capitalization, capital-accents, accents) and 1 orthographic, where both spellings are real words of the same recension and the edition rules which it prints. Substantive text agrees across both witnesses with zero further divergence.

adjudicated.ruling: Both spellings are real: ceno is the classical verb, and the ligature spellings cæno and cœno are the later ecclesiastical ones, all three headed by the dictionaries. The typical edition prints cenátum est in the Canon, and witness do follows it, so the edition prints that and records the hand missal's reading here rather than silently correcting a page that is not wrong. Whitaker's Words and Collatinus both head the classical spelling; Collatinus reads the ligature form under caeno.
The typical edition prints 'cálicem' where this edition prints 'Cálicem'; the reading is the same and only the case differs. Recorded rather than corrected.
Full stop closing the command to the disciples, with do and with the typical edition — parallel to the ruling at ordinarium.qui-pridie w035.

The typical edition sets the words of consecration in large MIXED CASE. Both other witnesses set capitals and this edition follows them: the capitals mark the consecration for a reader following the Mass, and two independent pages print them so. The reading is identical letter for letter — only the case differs. ON THE DISPUTED LIST for the expert: the authority prints mixed case.

House rule (ORTHOGRAPHY.md): accents ARE printed on capitals, and handmissal-eo attests the practice in exactly this place. Sánguinis has three syllables (the u of gui is a glide) and must show its stress. The same ruling governs the six entries that follow.
